title: AWS Lambda Now Runs GPU Inference with 48 Concurrent Invocations Sharing One Model per GPU
gist: AWS Lambda now runs GPU inference on EC2 G-series instances via Lambda Managed Instances, priced at EC2 On-Demand plus a 9.75% fee, with up to 48 concurrent invocations sharing one model copy per environment and prebuilt vLLM/SGLang images. Early tests show strong throughput (Gemma 4 E2B at 3,400–3,600 tokens/s at 48 concurrency) but friction from tooling gaps, zero default GPU quota, slow publish times and no P-family/Inferentia/Trainium support.

insights.claim: AWS Lambda Event Functions on Lambda Managed Instances can now run on EC2 G-series GPU instances (G4dn, G5, G6, G6f, Gr6, Gr6f, G6e at launch), generally available where both features exist, deployed as container images and triggered by standard Lambda event sources.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: AWS is pulling serverless GPU inference into its own ecosystem, pressuring third-party serverless GPU providers.
insights.locator: AWS has added GPU support to AWS Lambda

insights.claim: Lambda GPU functions are priced at the EC2 On-Demand rate plus a 9.75 percent management fee and $0.20 per million requests, versus a 15 percent fee on CPU instance types, with Savings Plans and Reserved Instances applicable and no duration charge.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: A lower management fee on GPUs plus RI/Savings Plan eligibility makes Lambda GPU cost-competitive and drives EC2 GPU consumption for AWS.
insights.locator: It is priced at the EC2 On-Demand rate

insights.claim: Because Lambda Managed Instances bill for the instance with no duration charge, a GPU instance bills as long as the minimum environment count is above zero.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Idle GPU cost persists unless minimum environments are set to zero — not pay-per-invocation economics.
insights.locator: The pricing model is the one Managed Instances introduced

insights.claim: AWS's Daniel Abib positions Lambda GPU against rival serverless GPU services that often sit outside the AWS environment without native event sources, identity or networking.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: AWS's moat argument is integration, a threat to standalone serverless GPU startups selling to AWS customers.
insights.quote: often sit outside your AWS environment, with no native event sources, identity, or networking.
insights.locator: The limits are in the launch post

insights.claim: On Lambda GPU, concurrent invocations in one environment share a single copy of the model in GPU memory, up to 48 per environment, with scaling driven by GPU utilization, CPU utilization and concurrency.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Model sharing across invocations improves GPU utilization economics versus one-request-per-container serverless designs.
insights.locator: Concurrent invocations in one environment share

insights.claim: Lambda capacity providers list allowed instance types and pick the newest generation with capacity, falling back to older generations when newer ones are short.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Automatic fallback hedges GPU scarcity but may yield variable performance.
insights.locator: A capacity provider lists the allowed instance types

insights.claim: Publishing a Lambda GPU version provisions environments, downloads weights and warms the engine before the first event, and Seekable OCI lazy loading can cut environment start time by up to 70 percent.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Pre-warming addresses cold-start concerns that have kept inference off serverless.
insights.locator: Publishing a version provisions the environments

insights.claim: AWS ships five Lambda GPU base images (CUDA only, CuPy, PyTorch, vLLM, SGLang); the vLLM and SGLang images need no handler code and swap models via a MODEL_ID pointing to Hugging Face, ModelScope, S3 or a local path.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Further entrenches vLLM and SGLang as default open inference servers in hyperscaler offerings.
insights.locator: AWS ships five GPU base images

insights.claim: Lambda GPU limits include container images up to 32 GB, 32 GB ephemeral storage, 2–32 GB memory, 3–48 GB accelerator memory, 15,000 vCPUs per capacity provider and up to 90-minute timeouts for asynchronous and event source mapping invocations.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: 48 GB accelerator ceiling confines Lambda GPU to small and mid-sized models.
insights.locator: The limits are in the launch post

insights.claim: Lambda Managed Instances still support only Event Functions, so the GPU path does not reach Lambda Web Functions, and AWS has not said whether it will.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: No HTTP-server GPU shape yet limits use for interactive streaming inference.
insights.locator: Managed Instances still support only Event Functions

insights.claim: Classmethod's Akaike found 37 of 81 accelerated instance types in us-east-1 accepted by Lambda GPU, all G-family; P-family, G7, Inferentia, Trainium, Graviton-based g5g and zip packages were refused.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Absence of Inferentia/Trainium and P-family means Lambda GPU currently drives Nvidia G-series demand, not AWS custom silicon.
insights.locator: The first hands-on reports came within a day

insights.claim: A PyTorch benchmark on Lambda GPU ran about 66 times faster on the Nvidia L4 than on the instance's CPU.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Confirms meaningful acceleration for small-model inference on entry GPUs.
insights.locator: A PyTorch benchmark ran about 66 times faster

insights.claim: At launch Terraform and the Cloud Control provider did not support Lambda's AcceleratorConfig, and a fresh AWS account's GPU vCPU quota is zero, requiring quota increases before use.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Infrastructure-as-code and quota friction will slow enterprise adoption in the near term.
insights.quote: if you use g6.xlarge (4 vCPU) with the default three instances, you need a quota of 12 vCPUs.
insights.locator: Still, neither Terraform nor the Cloud Control provider

insights.claim: An AWS Community Builder test served Gemma 4 E2B on one g6.2xlarge via the Lambda vLLM image, handling all 48 simultaneous requests and 417 of 417 calls successfully at roughly 130 tokens/s single-request and 3,400–3,600 tokens/s at 48 concurrency.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Batching on shared model copy gives ~26x aggregate throughput, making Lambda GPU viable for event-driven small-model inference.
insights.locator: A second test, by an AWS Community Builder

insights.claim: The same Lambda GPU test hit pipeline friction: 484 seconds from publish to active version, rejection of multi-platform Docker image indexes, and non-streamed replies preventing time-to-first-token measurement.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Slow deploys and no streaming limit Lambda GPU for chat-style workloads.
insights.locator: The friction was in the pipeline rather than the GPU

insights.claim: The tester concluded Lambda GPU is the simpler road for models behind events, queues or other AWS services, but recommended running vLLM on an EC2 G6 directly when streamed replies or full server control are needed.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Lambda GPU fits batch and event-driven inference; latency-sensitive chat still favors self-managed or specialist providers.
insights.quote: run vLLM on an EC2 G6 yourself.
insights.locator: When streamed replies or full control of the server are needed

insights.claim: Yan Cui's analysis holds that Managed Instances take tens of seconds to launch new EC2 instances, so Lambda GPU is not a good fit for large, unpredictable traffic spikes.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Spiky inference workloads remain better served by pre-provisioned capacity or other platforms.
insights.quote: it's not a good fit when you have large, unpredictable spikes in traffic.
